newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian retail, building data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian retail, building data.

text.p: Australian retail trade rose 0.8 percent in February, following a rise of 2.7 percent in January, official figures showed on Friday.
Seperate data showed building aprrovals fell 3.7 percent in February.
Economists forecasts had centred on a flat result for retail trade and a 2.0 percent fall in building approvals.
A selection of economists immediate rections to the data follows.
TIM PFITZNER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"(Retail) has come in at expectations, and we haven't had another big follow-up rise, although they were a bit stronger than we expected. It's certainly contrary to some of the anecdotal evidence that we have heard that the retail sector was still finding it pretty tough in the March quarter. Broadly across all the indicators we've got some consumer confidence coming back in the system, but we don't think that has delivered into overall rises in consumption."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"Retail trade is clearly in line with the anecdotal evidence that the pick-up in sales in January continued through to February. We weren't surprised to see a small correction in building approvals after the strong result in January. But the trend is still pointing to further gains ahead. Overall, it accords with our bullish growth outlook."
ANTHONY THOMPSON, ECONOMIST, HONG KONG BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"I am surprised by the strength of the retail trade numbers. I was expecting a pull-back, but a pull-back that would leave the trend accelerating. Up until we had this data, the trend was growing by 0.2 percent per month, now we have that rate of growth tripled. The impact of that on sentiment on the market has to outweigh the fact that building approvals undershot expectations. It gives a bearish tone to local markets, but I don't think we will get any substantial move until after the U.S. payrolls figures."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK OF AUSTRALIA

"Consumer spending has been the missing link in the economic recovery. It looks like it's coming back strongly. It also confirms what has already been anticipated -- that we are in for stronger economic growth in 1997."
IVAN COLHOUN, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, DEUTCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"The retail trade was stronger than people were expecting. And we expect a further considerable rise in the March figures. So the March quarter activity data is looking very strong at this stage. Yesterday's figures showed that as well, exports were strong and imports of consumption goods were also strong. It's starting to hang together very well for an economy on the improve. Building approvals were up ten percent last month so a drop of nearly four percent isn't huge in the scheme of things. It was a bit disappointing that it was in the private sector houses, but it wasn't too unexpected. Overall, the trend for construction is reasonably positive."
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK

"In terms of monetary policy looking further out, it's really on hold for quite sometime. Over the last six months retail trade has only grown 0.1 percent and in trend terms it's only starting to rise after falling late last year, and falls in retail trade are unprecedented. We've got an unemployment rate of 8.8 percent and it doesn't look as if there is going to be significant inroads until late in the year. And in terms of building approvals, we have seen a pick-up, but the pick-up that we have seen pales in comparison with previous pick-ups."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"Given the downward pressure on margins in the retail sector at the end of 1996 it's possible that the (retail sales) numbers that we've seen subsequently reflect, at least in part, price as well as volume. The figure today for building approvals serves as a reminder that it's not expected to be as strong a recovery in housing as we've seen in the previous housing cycles. In general I think the economy is picking up and for those who are not expecting a pick up until the second half of the year, well, they might have to revise some numbers a bit. I don't think any of the data we've seen this year warrants the expectation that monetary policy will be tightened in the second quarter, which I think the (interest rate) futures market has still got in there."
GUY BRUTEN, ECONOMIST, SBC WARBURG:

"Retail trade has been a lot stronger than we and many others thought. The anecdotal evidence pointed to a stronger start to the year than we'd thought, but we never expected it to be this strong. We're now looking at real growth in retail sales of 2.5 percent in the March quarter. That's very, very strong. Numbers like this indicate that we've passed a turning point in the economy and an acceleration is underway. It's not surprising to see Building Approvals come back after the strong set of numbers in the last month. The Reserve Bank are looking at (GDP) growth picking up to 4.0 to 4.5 percent by year end. These numbers just validate this view."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
